title: The bait
hook: the deer-feeder's crops, laid out to catch four herds

segments.voice: Yesterday: relay chariots, and your line, one stage at a time. Did you ride only the next chariot, and let the rest of the road wait? Day four hundred twenty-three.
screen: `RELAY CHARIOTS — ONE STAGE AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: A phone game is free. The first level is easy, the colors are bright, and there's a little gift waiting every morning if you open it. Nobody built that by accident. Somebody sat in a room and planned how you'd be caught, gently, so you'd never feel the net. Twenty-five centuries ago the Buddha described the same room, only with a field and a herd of deer. Today: the bait.
screen: `FREE, BRIGHT, A GIFT EVERY MORNING.` → `SOMEBODY PLANNED IT.` → `A FIELD, AND A HERD OF DEER.`

segments.voice: This is the twenty-fifth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings. A deer-feeder plants a crop, not out of kindness, but so deer will come, eat carelessly, and be easy to catch. Four herds come. The first herd walks straight into the crop, eats without care, grows heedless, and is caught. The second herd sees this and swears off the crop entirely. They go deep into the forest and live on wild grass. But in the last month of the hot season the grass and water run out. They grow thin and weak, wander back to the crop, eat wildly, and are caught too. The third herd is smarter. They make a lair close by and eat carefully, never losing their heads. But the deer-feeder notices them, puts up a great fence around the field, finds where they sleep, and catches them as well. The fourth herd makes its lair where the deer-feeder can't go. They eat without losing their heads, and slip away. The feeder and his men can't find them. Then the Buddha explains. The crop is the five cords of sense pleasure: sights, sounds, smells, tastes and touches that pull at us. The deer-feeder is Mara, the tempter. The herds are four kinds of seekers: those who dive in, those who run to harsh denial and break, those who stay close and get trapped by opinions, and those who go where Mara can't follow, into deep stillness. Notice the second herd. Running away wasn't enough. Starving wasn't freedom. The way out is neither the crop nor the desert. It's eating without being caught.
screen: `A CROP PLANTED TO CATCH DEER` · `FOUR HERDS: DIVE IN, RUN, HOVER, ESCAPE` · `THE CROP IS THE FIVE CORDS OF PLEASURE` · `RUNNING AWAY WASN'T ENOUGH` · then, large: `THE BAIT IS SET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one bait set for you. Sit, and think of the last time today you reached for something without deciding to: the phone, the fridge, the feed, the cart. Don't judge it. Just see the field it grew in: who planted it, and how bright it looked. Then come back to the breath, which nobody is selling you. Rest there. If the pull comes again during the sit, watch it rise like a deer lifting its head, and stay where you are. The bell holds the time.
The bait. The deer-feeder's crop: pleasures laid out on purpose, so we'll eat carelessly and be caught. Today's word.
Your line: the bait is set. Today, once, when something bright pulls at you, say the line quietly, and then choose: eat carefully, or walk on. Day four hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the Nivapa Sutta's four herds to describe the middle way between indulgence and harsh denial; monastics and lay meditators practice restraint of the senses and deep concentration as the 'lair' Mara can't reach.

match.prompt: the four herds — tap the pairs.
pairs: fled to the forest, starved, came back
ate carefully nearby, but was fenced in
went where the feeder couldn't follow

myth: the herd that gave up the crop completely escaped
the second herd starved in the hot season, came back weak, and was caught.
the crop is the five cords of sense pleasure, and the feeder is Mara.
the crop was planted to feed the deer
it was planted so the deer would grow careless and be easy to catch.

fork.setup: you're a deer. you've watched the first herd get caught in the crop. what do you do?
options: never touch the crop again, and live on wild grass.
eat carefully, from a lair close by.
eat without losing your head, from a lair the feeder can't reach.
fork.reveal: the second herd starved and came back; the third was fenced in. only the fourth herd, eating without infatuation where the feeder couldn't go, slipped away.

original.note: Pali nivapa: bait, fodder laid out. the discourse is the Nivapa Sutta.

trapdoor: what you thought: pleasure is the enemy.
what it means: the trap is eating carelessly; fleeing into harsh denial failed too.
what a scholar hears: the fourth herd's lair stands for the meditative absorptions (jhana), described in MN 25 as places where Mara loses sight of the practitioner.

notes: MN 25 paraphrased. The four herds as summarized: the third herd's fault in the sutta is views (the world is eternal etc.); the script compresses this to 'trapped by opinions'. Please confirm.
Pali nivapa (bait/fodder) and its Devanagari spelling: confirm.
The fourth herd's lair as the jhanas, where Mara is 'blindfolded': confirm the trapdoor wording.
